description: Turn-loop scenarios for the token-free end-to-end suite. THREE THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE EDITING. (1) Tool names and argument shapes are DATA, not contract: the adjudicator's and narrator's terminal tools are defined where those loops are configured, and this file follows them. Nothing in the stub reads these names. (2) Effect targets are six-part entity IDs, so they are bound to one world instance — org 'c360', namespace 'world1', template 'starter'. An end-to-end run under different instance config edits them here. (3) A verdict CANNOT choose the outcome band: it declares intents for all three and the seeded dice pick one. The miss/partial/full scenarios differ only in the narrator's voice, so the run that plays one must supply the campaign seed and turn id whose roll lands in that band. (4) Following from (3): the three bands touch THREE DIFFERENT PREDICATES on purpose (status, stamina, a relation), and none of them is a no-op against the starter world. That is what lets an end-to-end run assert WHICH band was committed rather than merely that something was — a band whose effect the world already satisfied would be indistinguishable from a batch that never ran.

roles.name: adjudicator
roles.description: The fiction adjudicator, on the mid model slot per F5. Matched on the endpoint's model name, which is deployment configuration, so a retarget to a live model is a model_registry edit.

roles.name: narrator
roles.description: The narrator, prose only, no mutation-capable tool. Matched the same way.

scenarios.name: no-roll
scenarios.description: The adjudicator declines the dice (D12: the reported gate is authoritative), so the verdict declares exactly one auto band and the turn resolves without a roll.

steps.description: Certain action, nothing at stake: Rook picks up the crowbar he is standing over.

arguments.rationale: Nobody is watching the supper and it is within arm's reach. There is nothing here for the dice to decide.

arguments.prose: The bread is still warm under the cloth. Rook takes it without breaking stride, and the winch keeps squealing behind him.

scenarios.name: miss
scenarios.description: A rolled turn narrated as a miss. The adjudicator step is identical across the three band scenarios by design — the band is the dice's answer, not the persona's — so the run must choose a seed and turn id that roll 6 or under.

modifiers.note: the crowbar bites on the winch housing

arguments.rationale: The winch will move for a crowbar, but not quietly, and the sentry is three strides away.

arguments.prose: The crowbar slips. Iron rings on iron, and Hollis has a hand on Rook's collar before the sound finishes crossing the yard.

scenarios.name: partial
scenarios.description: The same verdict, narrated as a 7-9. The run supplies a seed and turn id that roll into the partial band.

modifiers.note: the crowbar bites on the winch housing

arguments.rationale: The winch will move for a crowbar, but not quietly, and the sentry is three strides away.

arguments.prose: The gate lifts a hand's width and stops, and Rook is breathing hard through it. Wren does not look up from the winch, which is its own kind of answer.

scenarios.name: full
scenarios.description: The same verdict, narrated as a 10+. The run supplies a seed and turn id that roll into the full band.

modifiers.note: the crowbar bites on the winch housing

arguments.rationale: The winch will move for a crowbar, but not quietly, and the sentry is three strides away.

arguments.prose: The winch takes the crowbar like it was waiting for one. The gate comes up smooth and quiet, and for four long strides nobody in the yard is looking north.

scenarios.name: invalid-effect
scenarios.description: The rejection that actually reaches the APPLIER. Every value here is in the closed vocabulary and every field is the right shape, so the tool boundary accepts the exit — what it proposes is a character moved INTO AN ITEM, and a wrong-KIND target can only be refused by something that reads the graph. That is F16's own example. An out-of-vocabulary effect TYPE would be a shorter story: the terminal tool refuses it, the model gets a correction, and the applier never sees it — which is why this scenario is a kind violation and not a type one.

arguments.rationale: A character moved into a crowbar, proposed with total confidence — which is exactly how a model proposes one. Nothing in `world.location.current` says a location is a place.

steps.description: SCRIPTED AND NEVER CONSUMED — it is a trap, not a step. A refused batch fails the turn, `failed` is terminal, and the narration hop is gated on the effect-batch marker the applier never wrote. A call arriving here is the engine narrating a turn that did not happen, so the end-to-end suite asserts this script is untouched. Removing it would make that assertion unwritable: an engine that DID narrate would run off the end of an empty script and get a refusal, which is a different failure with a different message.

arguments.prose: Rook hesitates at the winch, and the moment passes. Nothing in the yard has changed.

scenarios.name: out-of-vocabulary-effect
scenarios.description: The OTHER rejection, and the pair matters: this verdict proposes an effect TYPE nobody registered, which the terminal tool refuses at the boundary — the model gets a correction it can act on and the applier never sees it. `invalid-effect` is its twin one layer down, where every value is in vocabulary and only the graph can say the target is the wrong KIND. A suite carrying only one of the two would prove one boundary and call it validation.

arguments.rationale: An effect type nobody registered, proposed with total confidence — which is exactly how a model proposes one.

scenarios.name: duplicate-delivery
scenarios.description: One turn's budget, exactly: one adjudication and one narration. The assertion IS the budget — a redelivered action that adjudicates twice runs off the end of this script and gets a refusal naming the role, instead of quietly buying a second call.

arguments.rationale: Nothing at stake; the interesting part of this turn is the delivery, not the judgment.

arguments.prose: Rook pockets the supper. Wren pretends to have seen nothing, which she is getting good at.

scenarios.name: crash-resume
scenarios.description: Same one-turn budget as duplicate-delivery, for the kill-and-restart cases. A resumed stage whose artifact ref already landed must NOT re-run its persona, and the proof is that this script still has an unconsumed step count of zero at the end rather than a second refusal.

modifiers.note: the crowbar bites on the winch housing

arguments.rationale: A rolled turn, so there is a phase between the verdict and the effects to be killed in.

arguments.prose: The gate gives, and Hollis decides — slowly, visibly — that he did not see which way the courier went.

scenarios.name: malformed-exit
scenarios.description: The adjudicator's first exit is structurally wrong — it reports a roll and then declares the single auto band a no-roll verdict would have — and its second is correct. Two steps on purpose: the tool boundary rejects the first with an invalid-argument error the model can self-correct from, so this scenario is what proves the rejection is a retry rather than a dead turn. Note the tool schema alone cannot catch this one; the coherence between requires_roll and the band set is a validator's job.

arguments.rationale: A verdict that calls for the dice and then declares the band set of a turn that did not.

steps.description: The corrected exit, after the tool boundary handed back an invalid-argument error.

modifiers.note: the sentry is already facing him

arguments.rationale: Same judgment, declared in a shape the engine can act on.

arguments.prose: Hollis moves first. The spear butt catches Rook across the ribs, and the crowbar rings off the cobbles somewhere behind him.

scenarios.name: never-terminates
scenarios.description: A persona that keeps reaching for context and never exits, so the loop's MaxIterations cap (M5) has something real to stop. The repeated step answers forever, which is the only way to tell a cap that works from a cap that was never reached.

scenarios.name: prose-instead-of-exit
scenarios.description: The adjudicator answers in prose and never calls its terminal tool. Nothing in the response is structured, so the executor's own handling — not the schema — is what has to catch it.

steps.content: Rook could probably lever the winch, though Hollis might notice. Let's say it's a 7 or better to get through.
